project: Local AI Document Assistant - Stage 1: local AI test page, then the LC check page
target_os: Windows 10/11 x64 (your current PC: Ryzen 5 3400G, 32 GB RAM, no dedicated GPU)
goal: Build one simple web page, with no login and no permissions, where you type a question and get an answer from a model running fully on your own PC. Then add an LC check page that compares a company's documents with the SWIFT LC (the source of truth). Login and the other big features come after that, phase by phase.

in_this_stage: Run llama.cpp (llama-server) on this PC with a small open model
Django page with a text box and an answer area
Streamed answers, timing numbers, simple settings
Offline and privacy check on Windows
Optional: saved chat history in SQLite
LC check v1: paste a SWIFT MT700 and a company document and see mismatches with exact highlights
not_in_this_stage: Login, users, roles, permissions (added after the LC check works and before anyone else can reach the app)
Document library, OCR for scans, embeddings, vector search
General comparison of many document types

principles: Small steps: every phase ends with something that works and a test you can run.
Everything stays on this PC. No cloud AI, no external API, no CDN, no telemetry.
Django and the model server listen on 127.0.0.1 only. Never 0.0.0.0.
Download software and models once, check them, then run offline. The app never downloads anything.
Write down measured numbers. Mark estimates as estimates.
Keep the page code behind one small function (ask_model) so the model or runtime can be swapped later.
Use only invented (synthetic) LC data for development. Never put real customer documents on this test setup.
assumptions: Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit, with an administrator account for the firewall step.
The PC has internet only during setup (downloads). After that it can be disconnected.
One user, one browser tab at a time (the CPU can only serve about one request at once).
Estimated day counts assume about 2 to 4 hours of work per day.

phases.name: Prepare the Windows PC
phases.goal: Know what the PC can do and install the basic tools.

steps.do: Record CPU, cores and RAM so every later benchmark has a baseline.
commands: Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors
steps.notes: Ryzen 5 3400G has 4 cores / 8 threads and supports AVX2 (no AVX-512). Check RAM is running dual-channel (two matching sticks); it affects answer speed.

steps.do: Install Python 3.12 (64-bit) from python.org and tick 'Add python.exe to PATH'. Install Git only if you want version control.
steps.notes: Use a Python version that Django and your libraries support at the time you start. Check this once.

steps.do: Create the folders from folder_layout.
commands: New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\local-ai\llama.cpp, C:\local-ai\models, C:\local-ai\app, C:\local-ai\notes, C:\local-ai\scripts

steps.do: Free disk space and close heavy programs while testing.
steps.notes: Windows itself uses roughly 3 to 4 GB of RAM (estimate). A 4B model at 4-bit needs about 2.5 GB, so RAM is not a problem for the first model.

steps.do: Make a notes file C:\local-ai\notes\model_register.md with columns: model name, source URL, licence, file name, SHA-256, date downloaded.

exit_criteria: py -3.12 --version prints a version
CPU and RAM details saved in notes
risks: Single-channel RAM makes answers slower; check and fix before judging the model.
results: Python 3.12.5 works (.venvDocument inside the Git project).
Folders created: C:\local-ai\llama.cpp, C:\local-ai\models; notes and scripts folders in the project.

phases.name: Run the model alone (no code yet)
phases.goal: Get a local model answering questions with only llama.cpp, before writing any Django code.

steps.do: Download the llama.cpp Windows x64 CPU build from the official ggml-org/llama.cpp GitHub releases page and unzip it into C:\local-ai\llama.cpp.
steps.notes: Pick the zip that says Windows x64 CPU. The exact file name changes with each release (it looks like llama-bNNNN-bin-win-cpu-x64.zip). Download only from the official repository. Write the release tag in your notes and do not auto-update.

steps.do: Download the model file Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M (about 2.5 GB) from the ggml-org/Qwen3-4B-GGUF page on Hugging Face (listed as Apache 2.0) and save it in C:\local-ai\models.
steps.notes: Download it in the browser, or use the -hf option once during setup only. Never use -hf from the app. Confirm the licence on the model card for the exact file you use.

steps.do: Check the file hash and record it.
steps.notes: Compare with the hash shown by the publisher if one is listed, and save it in model_register.md.

steps.do: Start the server on loopback only.
steps.notes: -c is the context size, -t is the number of CPU threads. Windows may show a firewall prompt the first time. Click Cancel or Block, because the server only needs loopback (127.0.0.1) and does not need to be reachable from other devices. If Windows SmartScreen warns about the exe, check that it came from the official release.

steps.do: Open http://127.0.0.1:8080 in your browser (llama-server has a small built-in chat page) and ask 5 simple questions.
steps.notes: Watch the startup log: it should list your CPU features (AVX2). Qwen3 may print a long 'thinking' section first. Add /no_think at the end of your question to turn this off for now (or check llama-server --help for a reasoning setting in your build).

steps.do: Check the health endpoint from a second PowerShell window.

deliverables: Model answers in the built-in chat page
exit_criteria: 5 questions answered correctly in plain English
Server only listens on 127.0.0.1 (check with: netstat -ano | findstr :8080)
Hash and licence saved in notes
risks: Missing DLL or crash on start: you probably downloaded the wrong build (GPU build instead of CPU). Use the CPU build.
Port 8080 already used: change --port and use the new port everywhere.

Server listens on 127.0.0.1:8080 only; /health returned ok.

phases.name: Measure speed and choose settings
phases.goal: Find out if the model is fast enough on this PC, using real numbers instead of guesses.

steps.do: Run the llama.cpp benchmark tool with 4 and 8 threads.
steps.notes: pp numbers are prompt reading speed (tokens per second). tg numbers are answer writing speed. Save the full output in notes.

steps.do: Create a fixed set of 6 test questions in C:\local-ai\notes\test_prompts.md and use the same set for every model.
steps.notes: Suggested set: (1) a short factual question, (2) a question with a pasted paragraph of about 500 words, (3) a question with a pasted text of about 2,000 words, (4) a question whose answer is not in the pasted text, (5) a name/date/amount extraction from pasted text, (6) a follow-up that depends on the previous answer.

steps.do: For each test question note: time to first word, total time, tokens per second, RAM used (Task Manager), and whether the answer was correct.
steps.notes: Use a table in your notes. Run each test twice; the first run includes loading time.

steps.do: Pick default settings: threads (4 or 8, whichever is faster), context size (start with 4096), temperature 0.2 to 0.3 for factual answers.
steps.notes: Do not use a huge context. Reading long text is the slow part on this CPU.

steps.do: Optional quick experiment: try the Windows x64 Vulkan build of llama.cpp with the Vega 11 integrated graphics and compare speed.
steps.notes: Gains are uncertain because the integrated GPU shares system RAM. Keep the CPU build as the default unless the numbers clearly improve and answers stay correct.

deliverables: Chosen thread count, context size, temperature
exit_criteria: You can state: 'on my PC this model reads X tokens/s and writes Y tokens/s'
You decided if the speed is acceptable for a test page
risks: Very slow reading of long prompts is normal on this CPU. Plan short prompts.
Other programs (browser tabs, antivirus scan) can distort results. Close them and repeat.

results.six_test_questions: All answered correctly, including saying a nominee is not mentioned in the document.
results.real_chat_speed: reading about 25 tokens/s; writing about 8 to 9.5 tokens/s; about 21 s to the first word for a 500-token document; follow-ups 3 to 5 s
decisions: Use 8 threads, context 4096 (raise to 8192 only if needed), one request at a time (-np 1).
Temperature 0.2 to 0.3 for factual answers in our own page.

phases.name: Minimal Django test page
phases.goal: One page: text box, Send button, answer area. No login, no database.
prerequisites: llama-server running on 127.0.0.1:8080 with the Phase 2 server command

steps.do: Use the existing virtual environment in your Git project and install the packages.
steps.notes: If PowerShell blocks the activate script, run once in this window: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. Commit requirements.txt to Git.

steps.do: Create the Django project and the chat app inside an app folder of your Git project.
Set safe local settings in config/settings.py.
steps.notes: ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['127.0.0.1', 'localhost']. Keep DEBUG on for now but never bind to 0.0.0.0. Read the model server address from one setting, LLAMA_SERVER_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:8080'. Keep Django's CSRF protection on and send the token with the page's fetch call.

steps.do: Write one small function ask_model(messages, temperature, max_tokens) in chat/llm_client.py that calls llama-server.
steps.notes: Use a timeout of several minutes because a long prompt can take a while on this CPU. Return a clear error message if the server is not running.

steps.do: Add two routes: GET / (the page) and POST /api/chat (returns JSON).
steps.notes: Page = one template with a textarea, a Send button and an answer box. Use plain JavaScript and no CDN. Save any CSS or JS in the app's static folder.

steps.do: Run Django and test.
steps.notes: Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in the browser.

request_body.message: What is the capital of France?
request_body.system: You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly in English.

response_body.reply: The capital of France is Paris.

messages.content: You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly in English.
What is the capital of France? /no_think

deliverables: Working page that returns a model answer
exit_criteria: A typed question returns an answer in the page
If llama-server is stopped, the page shows a friendly error and does not crash
Only 127.0.0.1 is used (check netstat -ano | findstr :8000)

Django dev server is only for local testing, not for real use.

phases.name: Streaming answers, settings and timing display
phases.goal: Make the page feel like a chat and show the numbers you need to judge the model.

steps.do: Switch to streaming: send 'stream': true to llama-server and pass the text to the browser piece by piece (Django StreamingHttpResponse; read the stream in the browser with fetch).
steps.notes: Test through runserver first. If words appear only at the end, a buffer is in the way; check for response buffering.

steps.do: Add a Stop button that cancels the request.
steps.notes: This matters on a CPU, because a wrong long answer wastes minutes.

steps.do: Add a small settings panel: system prompt, temperature, max answer length.
steps.notes: Keep defaults from Phase 2.

steps.do: Show timing under each answer: time to first word, total time, approximate tokens per second.
steps.notes: You can measure time in the browser. If the llama-server response includes a 'timings' section, show those values as well.

steps.do: Keep the conversation in the browser page memory and send the last few messages with each request (not the whole history).
steps.notes: A longer history means a longer prompt and a slower answer.

steps.do: Show 'Model is thinking...' while waiting and disable the Send button during a request.
steps.notes: One request at a time is the right design for this CPU.

steps.do: Escape the model's text before showing it in the page (use textContent, not innerHTML).
steps.notes: This prevents script injection from model output.

deliverables: Streaming chat page with Stop button, settings and timing
exit_criteria: First words appear while the answer is still being written
Stop button works
Timing line shown for every answer
risks: Streaming code is the trickiest part of this stage. Test with short prompts first.

phases.name: Offline and privacy check on Windows
phases.goal: Prove that nothing leaves your PC while you use the page.

steps.do: Block outbound internet for the two programs that matter, using Windows Firewall (run PowerShell as Administrator).
commands: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'LocalAI block llama-server out' -Direction Outbound -Program 'C:\local-ai\llama.cpp\llama-server.exe' -Action Block
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'LocalAI block python out' -Direction Outbound -Program 'C:\Users\My Local PC\Desktop\Selim\Document\.venvDocument\Scripts\python.exe' -Action Block
steps.notes: Loopback traffic (127.0.0.1) should still work. Test this. If the page stops working, check the rules and the program paths.

steps.do: Turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the network cable and use the page for 10 questions.
steps.notes: Everything must still work. This is your main offline proof.

steps.do: List the network connections of both programs while a question is running.
commands: Get-Process llama-server, python | Select-Object Id, ProcessName
steps.notes: Replace <pid> with each process ID. You should see only 127.0.0.1 connections and listening ports.

steps.do: Optional stronger proof: capture traffic with Wireshark while you use the page, with the network connected, and check there is no traffic from your programs to the internet.
steps.notes: Wireshark is free; install it on the PC only if you want this test.

steps.do: Check the code: no external URLs in templates or JavaScript, no CDN, no web fonts. Search your project for 'http' and 'https'.
Write what you tested and the results in notes\offline_test.md.
steps.notes: Be honest: this shows your two programs do not send data out. Windows itself, other programs and drivers still use the internet when it is connected. For a stronger claim, keep the PC offline.

deliverables: offline_test.md with date, steps and results
exit_criteria: The page works with the network disconnected
netstat shows only loopback connections for your two programs
No external URLs in the code
risks: Windows is not designed to be a locked-down offline server. A bank-level guarantee needs Linux and network-level controls later.

lc_check_plan.name: LC check (Letter of Credit document check)
lc_check_plan.why: Banks must check the documents a local company presents against the Letter of Credit that a foreign bank sent by SWIFT. Doing this by hand is slow and mistakes are costly. The tool should find mismatches quickly and point to the exact place on both sides.
lc_check_plan.when_to_build: Right after the normal Django frontend (Phases 3 and 4) works, and before any login or authentication system. The no-login version is only for one local PC with synthetic test data.
lc_check_plan.source_of_truth: The SWIFT LC (usually an MT700 message), plus any later amendments (MT707). Apply the amendments first, then compare.
lc_check_plan.side_to_check: The documents the local company presents (start with the commercial invoice; later bill of lading, packing list, certificate of origin and others that field 46A requires).
flow: Foreign (issuing) bank sends the LC as an MT700 to the local bank
Local bank advises it to the local company (the exporter)
Company prepares documents and presents them to the local bank
Local bank checks the documents against the SWIFT LC and reports discrepancies
lc_check_plan.design_idea: A separate LC Check page with two panes: the SWIFT LC (truth) on the left and the company document (to be checked) on the right, with a findings list in the middle or below. Clicking a finding highlights the matching text on both sides.
core_approach: MT700 is structured, so parse it by field tag with Python (not with the AI).
Extract the matching fields from the company document with rules first, and use the AI only where text is free-form.
Compare field by field in Python with explicit rules (exact, numeric tolerance, fuzzy name, date rules, normalised match).

Use the AI only for free-text clauses (goods description, additional conditions) and to explain each finding in plain words, and always check that the quoted evidence really exists in the source text.
Show evidence (page and position) for every finding. A human trade-finance officer makes the final decision.

fields_to_compare_v1.compare: currency exact; amount numeric, with the tolerance allowed by tag 39A if present
normalised and fuzzy name match; flag any difference for review
normalised and fuzzy name match; flag any difference for review
date rule (document dates must be on or before expiry)

fields_to_compare_v1.field: Port of loading / port of discharge

fields_to_compare_v1.compare: AI check with quoted evidence, plus rules for quantity, unit price and total; officer reviews
checklist: is each required document present
AI check of each condition with quoted evidence; always shown to the officer
condition check against the shipping document

cautions: Not every difference is a real discrepancy. Trade rules allow some tolerance, so the tool flags and classifies; the officer decides.

The exact discrepancy rules and tolerances must come from the bank's own trade-finance policy and the standard rules it follows (for example UCP 600 practice). Confirm them with a trade-finance officer before treating results as final.
OCR errors can create false mismatches, so show the page image beside each finding and a confidence score.
Use only invented (synthetic) LCs and documents for development and testing. Never use real customer data on this test setup.
The tag list above is the common MT700 field set and must be confirmed against the bank's SWIFT message guide.
lc_check_plan.speed_note: The model reads about 25 tokens per second on this PC (measured). Every AI call on a 600-token document costs roughly 25 seconds of reading before the first word (calculated from the measured speed). So do as much as possible in Python and call the AI only for a few free-text fields.
lc_check_plan.position_in_order: After Phase 4, before Phase 5 and before any login system
lc_check_plan.v1_scope: SWIFT MT700 text (pasted) versus a commercial invoice (pasted text); invented data only; no login. v1.1 adds upload of TXT, DOCX and text PDF.

steps.name: Make synthetic test data
steps.do: Write 3 invented MT700 messages and, for each, a matching commercial invoice. Then make copies of each invoice with one seeded error at a time.
seeded_error_types: buyer or seller name spelled differently
amount higher than the LC amount
LC number with one changed digit
invoice dated after the expiry date
shipment date after the latest shipment date
different port of loading or discharge
goods description with a changed quantity or item
steps.deliverable: A tests/lc_samples folder with the files and an answer key (which error is in which file)
steps.exit_criteria: At least 20 test pairs with a written answer key

steps.name: MT700 parser
steps.do: Write a Python function that reads MT700 text and returns its fields by tag (20, 31D, 32B, 39A, 43P, 43T, 44C, 44E, 44F, 45A, 46A, 47A, 48, 50, 59 and so on), including multi-line fields. Add a function that applies an MT707 amendment on top.
steps.exit_criteria: All fields from the sample MT700 files are parsed correctly; the amendment test passes

steps.name: Extract fields from the company document
steps.do: For the commercial invoice, extract the LC reference, buyer, seller, amount, currency, goods description, quantity, ports and dates. Use rules and regular expressions first. Use the AI with a JSON-only answer format for the fields that rules cannot find. Store each value with its source location.
steps.exit_criteria: Correct values on the sample invoices, each with the page or line where it was found

steps.name: Comparison engine
steps.do: Normalise values (case, spaces, accents, titles, date and number formats). Compare each field with its rule from fields_to_compare_v1 and give a status. Check that required documents are listed. Keep the rules in one configuration file so the bank can adjust them.
steps.exit_criteria: Every seeded error in the test data is reported with the right status and field

steps.name: LC Check page (no login yet)
steps.do: Build a Django page with two panes (SWIFT LC on the left, company document on the right). v1: paste text into each box. v1.1: upload TXT, DOCX or text PDF. Show a findings table; clicking a finding highlights the matching text on both sides.
steps.exit_criteria: A user can paste an MT700 and an invoice and see the findings with highlights

steps.name: AI explanation and officer decision
steps.do: For each finding, ask the model to explain it in one or two plain sentences using only the two values and their surrounding text. Check that any quoted text exists in the source. Let the officer mark each finding as accepted discrepancy, not a discrepancy, or needs more information, and save the decision.
steps.deliverable: Explanations and a saved decision per finding
steps.exit_criteria: Explanations never invent values; decisions are stored and shown again after a restart

steps.name: Measure and write the result
steps.do: Run all test pairs. Record per error type how many were found (recall) and how many wrong flags there were (precision), plus time per check.
steps.exit_criteria: Numbers for every error type; a list of what was missed and why

lc_check_plan.test_plan: Run all seeded-error pairs, report recall and precision for each error type, and record the time per check.
open_questions: Besides the documents, does the company also give a typed copy of the LC that must be checked?
Which documents should version 1 cover after the commercial invoice (bill of lading, packing list, certificate of origin)?
Which discrepancy rules and tolerances does the bank apply (and which written policy should be followed)?
Do real documents arrive as scans, text PDFs or Word files?
How are MT707 amendments delivered and should the tool apply them automatically?
